strengths: Addresses a genuinely practical and underexplored problem (channel-wise asynchronous sampling, test-time missing values, inter-channel dependencies) with strong real-world motivation and theoretical justification (Appendix B on spectral distortion from interpolation)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including: multiple practical scenarios, artificially constructed and real-world datasets, extensive ablations (5.2, Appendix C), robustness analyses (input length variation, frequency preservation), and error bars from 5 random seeds

Elegant unified framework combining three related challenges with well-designed components: channel tokens for variable-length representation, frequency-adaptive patching, and tailored masked attention strategy
Consistent experimental improvements across all datasets and scenarios (Tables 1-2, 13-14) with thorough ablation studies demonstrating necessity of each component
Demonstrated applicability beyond the proposed setting: evaluation on conventional multivariate forecasting (Table 11) shows competitive performance with standard time series methods
Inclusion of real-world industrial dataset (LNG Cargo Handling System) with practical relevance to shipping operations
Frequency-domain analysis (Section 6.3, Table 6) provides signal processing justification, showing CTF better preserves spectral characteristics compared to interpolation-based baselines
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (learnable summarization tokens, FFT-based adaptive patching, masked attention, patch masking) are well-established; primary contribution is their combination for a specific problem setting rather than fundamental innovation

Critical scalability limitations that severely restrict practical impact: O(T²) attention complexity where T = Σ(L⁽ⁱ⁾ + C) becomes prohibitive for high-dimensional systems; acknowledged but unresolved; most industrial systems have 50+ channels but experiments use only 10; no computational cost comparisons provided

Artificial dataset construction: 'practical' versions of standard benchmarks use ad-hoc resampling choices (why these specific periods?); unclear representativeness of constructed asynchrony patterns compared to real-world systems; real-world CHS dataset is small and domain-specific (shipping only)

Unfair baseline comparisons: (1) CTF actually uses forward-fill preprocessing for 'input shape compatibility' despite claiming to be interpolation-free, (2) baselines trained on linearly interpolated data but tested with zero-filling creates asymmetry that conflates benefits of avoiding interpolation with benefits of explicit masking, (3) methods designed for irregular sampling not included in direct comparisons

FFT-based patching lacks robustness analysis: no evaluation of failure modes when peak frequency detection fails (non-stationary signals, multiple dominant frequencies, noisy signals); fallback strategy only mentioned without detail; real-world signals often have complex spectra where single peak frequency is suboptimal

Technical clarity issues: decoder architecture ('shared per sampling period') inadequately explained; channel token initialization not specified; parameter counts not provided despite efficiency claims; behavior when channels have very few patches after masking not discussed

Acknowledged but unresolved metric limitations: authors note in Section G that MSE/MAE may fail to capture structural fidelity for asynchronous time series but paper does not explore alternative metrics; modest improvements (often 1-5%) on standard metrics don't strongly demonstrate practical value

Incomplete analysis of edge cases: no investigation of failure modes; no sensitivity analysis for FFT parameters; no explicit evaluation of scalability degradation with increasing channel count; limited details on CHS dataset characteristics (only 10/52 channels used, selection criteria unclear)

Limited comparison with irregular time series methods: related work cites specialized methods for truly irregular sampling but paper doesn't include direct experimental comparisons; distinction from irregular sampling setting could be sharper

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing three simultaneously occurring challenges (asynchrony, missingness, dependencies) that existing work handles only in isolation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with diverse baselines (channel-dependent, independent, irregular, missing-aware methods) and thorough ablation studies showing contribution of each component
Sound technical design: unified mask-guided attention elegantly handles intra- and cross-channel interactions; channel tokens provide useful abstraction for heterogeneous sampling
Consistent empirical improvements across all datasets and conditions (various prediction lengths, missing ratios); sometimes substantial margins (e.g., EPA results)

Excellent supplementary materials with theoretical analysis of interpolation-induced spectral distortion (Appendix B), detailed scalability analysis (up to 275 channels), and extensive implementation details

Robustness demonstrations: model generalizes to different input lengths without retraining (Table 5), maintains performance across missing ratios (Table 2), and ablations show each component contributes
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: channel tokens similar to iTransformer/TimeXer, frequency-based patching builds on Moirai/LightGTS, patch masking adapted from PatchDropout; contribution is primarily a combination of existing techniques

Potentially unfair baseline comparisons: regular baselines require interpolation but paper doesn't thoroughly isolate whether improvements stem from avoiding interpolation vs. architectural superiority; only TimeXer analyzed in detail (Section 6.3); some baselines (ContiFormer, Hi-Patch) were reimplemented rather than original implementations

Artificial and limited real-world validation: asynchronous datasets are synthetic adaptations of regular benchmarks via manual resampling; only one private industrial dataset (LNG CHS) with modest gains; real-world asynchrony typically involves irregular timestamps, not fixed sampling periods

Significant scalability limitations: out-of-memory at 280 channels on 24GB GPU (Table 12); industrial/IoT systems often have hundreds or thousands of channels; quadratic attention complexity not addressed

Insufficient analysis of cross-channel dependencies: unclear when/why dependencies matter; Section 6.1 shows optimal tokens vary (1-3) by dataset but provides no insight into what types of dependencies are learned or captured

Problem setting concerns: distinction from highly sparse irregular time series methods (Raindrop, Hi-Patch) is unclear; fixed sampling periods differ from operational asynchrony with variable delays and jitter; no evaluation on public irregular time series benchmarks

FFT-based frequency detection (Appendix A.2) uses arbitrary 70th percentile threshold with no sensitivity analysis; fails for non-periodic/short sequences; fallback mechanism poorly explained; robustness to noisy signals unclear
Loss function limitations: authors acknowledge (Section G) that MSE may favor overly smoothed predictions and cannot penalize amplitude attenuation over longer horizons, but provide no solutions

Inconsistent experimental setup: different learning rates per dataset (10^-4 to 10^-2) complicate comparison; maximum 10 epochs with early stopping is short; train/test split details insufficient; error bars in main tables relegated to appendix

Missing key ablations: sensitivity to FFT threshold, random masking ratio, and channel token count; effect of positional embeddings; importance of avoiding interpolation vs. architectural choices remains unclear

strengths: Well-motivated problem combining three practical challenges (asynchrony, missingness, cross-channel dependencies) that existing methods don't address simultaneously
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 6 datasets, multiple baseline architectures, ablation studies, and attention visualization
Thoughtful mask-guided attention design allowing structured intra-channel and cross-channel information flow
Thorough documentation with detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, and reproducibility information
Real-world LNG dataset (CHS) provides practical grounding beyond modified benchmarks
Consistent empirical improvements across datasets with error bars from multiple seeds
Good analysis of frequency-domain effects of interpolation (Appendix B)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: channel tokens from iTransformer/TimeXer, FFT-based patching from Moirai/LightGTS, patch masking from PatchDropout. Main contribution (mask-guided attention) is incremental combination of existing techniques

Unfair experimental setup: Regular baselines must use linear interpolation due to architectural constraints, while CTF uses masking. Advantage partly comes from preprocessing difference rather than architectural superiority. No fair comparison with all methods using identical preprocessing
Contradictory 'interpolation-free' claim: Appendix A.2 explicitly states forward-fill interpolation is used during preprocessing; the positioning as interpolation-free is misleading

Weak real-world validation: Most datasets are artificially modified benchmarks (ETT, Weather, SolarWind). Only one truly real dataset (CHS) from single domain with arbitrary selection of 10 channels. Generalization to other domains unclear

Modest and potentially insignificant improvements: 0.8-5.5% gains on many datasets; no statistical significance testing despite error bars. Some improvements disappear on specific metrics (e.g., CHS CMAE shows <2% gain)
Weak ablation study: Removing patch masking changes metrics only 1.3% (Table 3), contradicting its claimed importance. Suggests component contributions are not well-established
Arbitrary design choices without principled justification or ablation: FFT threshold (70th percentile), number of channel tokens (requires per-dataset tuning), patch masking ratio (0.4)
Scalability limitation: Out-of-memory at 280 channels (Table 12). Many real systems exceed this; limitation not adequately emphasized. Quadratic attention complexity limits practical applicability

Artificial test-time missing setup: Contiguous block-wise missingness doesn't reflect real patterns where failures are sporadic or correlated. Evaluation may not generalize to real-world missing patterns

Problematic baseline selection: Irregular-sampling methods (Hi-Patch, ContiFormer) designed for highly sparse point-wise data, not structured multi-rate asynchrony. These baselines may not be appropriate comparisons
Number of channel tokens (Table 4) varies significantly across datasets (1-3) with no principled selection method for new datasets. This critical hyperparameter requires expensive tuning

Frequency bias analysis (Appendix B) is lengthy but tangentially connected to main results. Doesn't clearly explain why frequency preservation translates to the modest performance improvements observed
Missing statistical rigor: No significance tests despite reporting error bars. Many improvements are within noise margins
Limited analysis of when/why method works: No breakdown of which channel-pairs benefit from interactions, performance as asynchrony increases, or failure modes
No computational cost comparison (runtime, memory, inference latency) with baselines reported
Evaluation metric (CMSE) averages across channels with different prediction lengths, potentially masking dataset-specific performance variations

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing three simultaneous challenges (asynchrony, missingness, dependencies) that existing methods handle separately
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 10+ baselines, multiple datasets, thorough ablations, error bars, and multiple runs demonstrating solid empirical methodology
Clear technical presentation with excellent reproducibility details, promised code release, and thorough appendices covering implementation, datasets, and additional analyses
Insightful spectral analysis (Appendix B) theoretically justifying the avoidance of interpolation through frequency-domain distortion characterization
Consistent empirical improvements across all datasets and missing ratios, with robustness analysis including input length variation (Table 5) and scalability testing (Table 12-13)
Unified mask-guided attention elegantly combines intra-channel local modeling and cross-channel global interactions without separate modules
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—primarily combines existing techniques (frequency-based patching from Moirai/LightGTS, channel tokens from iTransformer, patch masking from PatchDropout) rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts

Artificial evaluation setting with four of six main datasets being resampled versions of existing benchmarks; only one truly real-world dataset (LNG-CHS), raising questions about whether resampled asynchrony patterns match real-world scenarios

Evaluation fairness concerns: regular baselines use interpolation while CTF avoids it (preprocessing advantage); all baselines receive zero-filled missing values potentially misaligned with their design; CMSE treats all channels equally without importance weighting

Architectural scalability limitations with quadratic attention complexity failing at ~280 channels; only tested up to 275 channels; proposed solutions relegated to Discussion section without implementation

Incomplete methodological justifications: FFT threshold (70th percentile) unexplained; channel token count requires per-dataset tuning with unclear pattern (Table 4); fallback patching mechanism vague; masking ratio (0.4) lacks principled justification

Evaluation fairness: Modified TimeXer (Table 14) shows marginal improvements in some cases (e.g., ETT2: 0.377 vs 0.374), suggesting gains may partly reflect preprocessing rather than pure modeling advantages

Missing technical depth: no visualization of learned dependencies; limited analysis of which patterns the model captures; redundancy in attention masking variants (CD-ReadOnly and CD-ReadOnly-Indexed identical in Table 11) unexplored

Unresolved acknowledged limitations: amplitude attenuation over long horizons persists; MSE loss suboptimal for time series—both identified as problems but not addressed; future work promised but not delivered
